articles.title: 28 years in jail for 2 Indian-origin men whose high-speed race killed UK mum, daughter
articles.summary: Two Indian-origin men have been jailed for a total of 28 years after their high-speed driving led to the deaths of a 27-year-old mother and her
articles.body: Two Indian-origin men have been jailed for a total of 28 years after their high-speed driving led to the deaths of a 27-year-old mother and her four-year-old daughter in Leeds, northern England, in January 2023. Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, while Jasskamal Riyat, 37, received a 16-year term at Leeds Crown court on Monday.Bhachu pleaded guilty to causing the deaths of Justyna Hulboj and her daughter, Lena Czepczor, by dangerous driving. Riyat was convicted of the same offences after a trial in August. Both men were also handed six-year driving bans and will have to take an extended driving test before they can drive again."A road is not a race track. A powerful car is not an invitation to test its limits on a public road," Judge Ray Singh said while sentencing the men. "The consequences of competitive driving at extreme speed can be, and in this case were, irreversible," he added.The collision took place on January 16, 2023, when Bhachu lost control of his Audi and struck Justyna and Lena as they walked to school in Leeds. The car then crashed into the wall of the Vertu Jaguar Leeds dealership on Scott Hall Road. Both mother and daughter died at the scene.According to the BBC, prosecutors told Riyat's trial that he had been driving at 89mph on a road with a 40mph speed limit shortly before the collision. He was driving a BMW 1 Series and was allegedly racing Bhachu's Audi TT RS.The BBC reported that Riyat was also holding his phone and recording Bhachu as he accelerated away from traffic lights, saying: "Watch this guy let it off." The two men did not know each other but had earlier lowered their windows to speak at traffic lights.Riyat denied racing Bhachu. According to the BBC, he initially told police he had been "doing a steady 40" and later suggested he might have exceeded the speed limit because he was travelling to a work meeting. After watching footage in court, he revised his estimate to 50mph.The BBC also reported that Riyat was forced to stop because of the wreckage after the collision. He took photographs before driving around the scene and continuing to work. The jury took less than two hours to convict him on two counts of causing death by dangerous driving.West Yorkshire Police identified Riyat as the driver of a black BMW 135i using dashcam and CCTV footage supplied by members of the public. Bhachu's own dashcam captured a conversation between the two men at traffic lights, during which Bhachu boasted that his Audi had 560 horsepower and that he had only been using quarter throttle.“Bhachu and Riyat didn’t know each other. They were two men showing off their fast cars on a busy dual carriageway," Detective Inspector Paul Conroy, of West Yorkshire Police’s Major Collision Enquiry Team, said.“Ultimately, Bhachu thought he could drive at those speeds in his high-powered car, but he couldn’t, and his loss of control took two lives and ruined many more.“Riyat witnessed this collision but instead of stopping to check if those involved were okay, he left the scene. He denied his involvement but was convicted thanks to the extensive footage showing his speeding vehicle in the moments leading up to the collision,” he added.“A woman and her young daughter have died because of the actions of these men, and I know no sentence will ever feel enough to compensate for the lives that have been lost," Conroy said.“This sentencing hearing though does mark the end of a long criminal justice process for Justyna and Lena’s family.“It is over two years since Bhachu admitted his part in this tragic incident and I know that the wait for justice has taken its toll. My thoughts are firmly with them today,” he said.In a statement, Justyna's fiancé and Lena's father said his “whole world collapsed in one second” after the crash.“Every day I feel a huge void after their departure, and I imagine what it would be like if they were still alive. We had so many plans and dreams and in one moment it all ended... This nightmare will last for the rest of my life," he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Iranian women have launched a campaign pledging their wedding rings as a symbolic reward for revenge against US President Donald Trump, with hundreds gathering in Tehran to express their support for retribution following recent wars.According to Iranian newspaper Tehran Times, the campaign, called ‘Rings of Revenge’, was launched by a group of women under the name ‘Madaraaneh’ (Maternal). The initiative was unveiled alongside a gathering titled ‘Rastakhiz of Tehran Women’, or ‘The Uprising of the Women of Tehran’, held on Thursday night, October 22, outside the main gate of the University of Tehran.Hundreds of women from different walks of life attended the gathering, including students, volunteers and the wives and daughters of those killed in the two recent wars. The programme featured speeches by women activists, choir performances and elegies, with revenge emerging as its central theme.The participants also joined the ‘Golden Retribution’ campaign, which encourages donations of gold and money to support what organisers describe as efforts to secure revenge. The Nehzat-e Madari movement, which runs the drive, has reportedly gifted gold donors bracelets bearing a bullet-shaped plaque as a reminder of their stated mission.Tehran Times reported that the organisers view retribution for the killing of Iran's former leader as a mission, with the donated jewellery serving as a symbol of their commitment.Since the war began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has lost several key political, military and security figures, dealing a major blow to the country’s leadership. Among those killed were Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, national security chief Ali Larijani and senior commanders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).The campaign comes amid continuing tensions across the Middle East, with Iran's relations with the US and Israel remaining a major source of regional uncertainty. The wider conflict has also involved the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, who have continued to launch attacks against targets they describe as linked to their adversaries.Meanwhile, Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz on Monday denied reports of a rift between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the military leadership over a possible operation against Iran ahead of Israel's national elections. articles.title: ‘Will respond to legitimate demands’: Macron moves to ease France’s student unrest; vows 'concrete measures'
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that the government would announce concrete measures to address students' demands for better learning
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that the government would announce concrete measures to address students' demands for better learning conditions and more resources after weeks of protests, school blockades and demonstrations continue to fuel unrest across the country.Macron said Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu would announce “strong measures” after meeting student unions. However, he warned that further unrest remained a possibility, with more protests expected next Saturday.“I have also asked the government to respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement,” Macron told reporters during a visit to Marseille in southern France.The government is expected to announce changes to Parcoursup, France's national online university admissions platform, French media reported. Students have criticised its selection criteria, arguing that they lack transparency and limit equal access to their preferred courses.Their demands also include more teachers to cover staff absences, school renovations, changes to teaching hours and smaller classes. The government announced on October 8 that it would deploy 3,000 additional substitute teachers to high schools facing staffing shortages.The protests began with high school blockades in mid-September and have since spread nationwide. Students have accused the government of failing to address their concerns over poor school conditions and inadequate resources.Demonstrations on October 17 against rising living costs and poor school conditions turned violent, with groups setting fires, looting shops, storming public buildings and clashing with police. Protesters also briefly stormed Marseille City Hall during the unrest.A subsequent round of nationwide demonstrations on Saturday saw less violence. Authorities estimated that more than 400,000 people took part, while organisers put the turnout at nearly 800,000.The unrest has also led to mass arrests and renewed scrutiny of police crowd-control weapons, which have been blamed for causing life-changing injuries to some teenagers.The demands for better-funded schools, particularly in poorer communities, come as France faces record poverty and mounting public debt.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a major relief for local commuters, residents living within 20 km of a National Highway toll plaza can now opt for an annual concessional
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a major relief for local commuters, residents living within 20 km of a National Highway toll plaza can now opt for an annual concessional pass costing Rs 1,500 for plazas located outside municipal or local town limits and Rs 3,000 for those within such limits. Currently, eligible residents can obtain a monthly pass for Rs 360, amounting to Rs 4,320 annually.Road transport ministry notified the changes to NH Fee Rules on Monday. Under the provision, vehicle owners with valid and functional FASTags registered for personal use can choose either the existing monthly pass or the new concessional local pass for commuting through the specific toll plaza.Govt will revise these rates every year on April 1. As per the notification, the concession will be applicable only to the specific toll plaza and will not be transferable for use at other plazas. However, the pass will not be issued for NHs or expressways where toll is collected under a closed user fee collection system.The rules also make the concession conditional on the non-availability of a service road or alternative road for the vehicle owner or driver. articles.title: Wisconsin Rapids rejected a data centre plan for a former paper mill; the 1.2 million sq ft project now faces a year-long development freeze
articles.summary: Wisconsin Rapids, a city in the US state of Wisconsin, has rejected a proposal to transform a former paper mill site into a large data centre, ending
articles.body: Wisconsin Rapids, a city in the US state of Wisconsin, has rejected a proposal to transform a former paper mill site into a large data centre, ending months of debate over the future of the property. On October 20, 2026, the city's Common Council voted unanimously against the development permit, following concerns about the application and opposition from local residents. The decision comes as the city implements a year-long moratorium on new data centre developments, giving officials time to review local rules before considering similar projects in the future.Wisconsin Rapids declined the former paper mill data centre planAccording to WXPR's report, the Common Council voted 7-0 to reject the conditional use permit for the proposed hyperscale data centre. The project was planned for the site of the former paper mill, which had been a major part of the city's economy for more than a century.The decision followed an earlier recommendation from the city's Planning Commission, which voted unanimously against the application in September. Concerns centred on missing information and whether the developer had provided sufficient details to demonstrate that the proposal met the city's requirements.As reported by Civic Media, the commission identified gaps relating to electrical utility approvals, staffing plans, construction traffic and building layouts. The developer disputed the findings, maintaining that it had responded to the city's questions.The Common Council's final decision meant the application could not proceed under the proposed permit. It also reflected the wider debate about how the city should manage large technology developments and assess their potential effects on the surrounding community.What was planned for the former paper mill siteThe proposal was submitted by PNK Group USA, which sought to redevelop approximately 209 acres of the former mill property at 950 Fourth Avenue North. According to Civic Media, the planned campus would cover around 1.2 million square feet, combining the renovation of an existing building with the construction of four additional buildings.The development was intended to accommodate large-scale computing operations, including those associated with artificial intelligence. The proposed facility was expected to require approximately 150 megawatts of electricity, making power supply an important consideration in the planning process.The location was attractive to developers because of the infrastructure already available at the industrial property. Wisconsin Public Radio explained that the former mill had connections to electricity, roads, railways and other essential networks.However, the site's industrial history did not guarantee approval for a new development. The application still had to satisfy the city's planning requirements, while residents and officials sought greater clarity about the proposed facility and its potential long-term effects.The former paper mill became available for redevelopmentThe site has a long history in Wisconsin Rapids, where the paper industry shaped local employment and community identity. The mill opened in 1894 and became one of Wisconsin's largest paper-making operations.According to WPR, the facility specialised in glossy magazine paper during its later years. However, declining demand for that product contributed to its closure in 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic. The shutdown left nearly 1,000 people without jobs, marking a significant economic change for the city.Attempts to restart the mill or find a buyer were unsuccessful, and the industrial buildings were demolished in 2025. The cleared property subsequently became a potential site for redevelopment.WPR reported that a data centre proposal first emerged in December 2025. Interest in the site grew partly because of its existing electrical capabilities and its previous industrial use.Although the property offered an opportunity to attract new investment, its future became a source of disagreement. Some residents wanted a development that would create employment while addressing local priorities, rather than automatically accepting a large data centre as the next use for the land.Concerns raised by residents about the projectOpposition to the proposal developed over several months. According to WXPR, members of South Wood County Neighbors for Responsible Development organised against the development, attending meetings and working to prevent the project from moving forward.Residents raised concerns about noise and the potential effects of increased electricity demand on local energy costs. Questions also arose about the project's environmental implications and whether the information supplied by the developer was sufficient to assess its impact.The group formed in April 2026, and its campaign continued through public meetings and discussions with local officials. Marissa Johnson, a member of the organisation, told WXPR that opposing the proposal had become a sustained effort over the preceding 6 months.The developer also held meetings to explain the proposed facility and outline its potential benefits. Civic Media reported that PNK Group promoted the possibility of new jobs and investment, alongside a proposed $5.7 million community benefits plan.That plan included funding for public waterfront access, emergency response services, workforce training and river protection.How will the year-long development freeze affect future proposalsThe rejection of the permit comes alongside a separate decision to pause new data centre development. WXPR reported that Wisconsin Rapids introduced a one-year moratorium on October 9, 2026, with the option of extending it to 18 months.The restriction prevents new data centre proposals from proceeding while the moratorium remains in effect. City officials intend to use the period to review existing ordinances and determine whether additional rules are needed to assess future applications.Mayor Matt Zacher told WXPR that he was not opposed to all data centres but believed the city needed to take its time to ensure that developments were planned properly. He warned that a poorly designed facility could affect the community for decades.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: IISER Pune withdraws Umar Khalid’s book “Fractured Communities” from its library after social media backlash, citing precaution to avoid unrest and unrest.
articles.body: Pune: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Pune has withdrawn ‘Fractured Communities’, a book based on the PhD thesis of jailed activist and former JNU researcher Umar Khalid, after its inclusion in the Srinivasa Ramanujan Library triggered a social media controversy over the weekend.The institute said the book was retracted “as a precaution in order to avoid any misunderstanding or unrest” after the matter was brought to the authorities’ attention. “The book collection at the institute library is built through recommendations from institute members, and a dedicated committee oversees the functioning of the library. On average, over 50 books from various areas are routinely added every month to the library,” the institute said in a statement.“Regarding the book in question, as soon as the matter was brought to the attention of institute authorities, it has been decided to retract the book as a precaution in order to avoid any misunderstanding or unrest. The institute will examine what further action or steps can be taken,” the statement read.The controversy began after a photograph of the book displayed on the library’s digital board under the title ‘New Additions of Books’ was shared on ‘X’ by the handle @GemsofAcademia on Saturday night. The post was widely shared, with Madabhushi Madan Gopal, chairperson of the institute’s board of governors, responding through his personal ‘X’ account.“As in-charge chairperson, BoG, IISER Pune, I am shocked to know this. This is retracted last night and action is initiated on those who played this mischief. I assure such things will not happen again in IISER Pune. Prof. Sunil Bhagwat, Director, has taken immediate steps. We need to be alert,” he wrote.In a subsequent post, Gopal said the institute had identified the person responsible for this and that prompt action had been initiated. “There should be suitable remedial measures,” he posted.Asked about the action referred to in Gopal’s posts, an IISER Pune official said the chairperson had tweeted in his personal capacity through his personal account.The controversy divided opinion online, with a section criticising a central science institute for recommending the book, while another defended it as a researched work on Adivasis.‘Fractured Communities: Adivasi Histories and the Politics of Power’, released earlier this year, examines the history of Singhbhum’s tribal societies and is based on Khalid’s PhD thesis at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). Khalid has been lodged in Delhi’s Tihar Jail since 2020 as an undertrial prisoner in connection with a case registered under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) and other provisions of law. articles.title: E100 flex-fuel vehicles get regulatory push ahead of launch
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Paving the way for roll out of flex fuel vehicles (FFVs) that can run on up to E100 — nearly 100% pure ethanol or about 93-95% ethanol-blended
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Paving the way for roll out of flex fuel vehicles (FFVs) that can run on up to E100 — nearly 100% pure ethanol or about 93-95% ethanol-blended with petrol — road transport ministry Monday modified changes in Central Motor Vehicles Rules.This comes barely months before some car manufacturers launch their E100 models.FFVs with an internal combustion engine can run on petrol, biofuels like ethanol or methanol, or any mixture of both stored in a single fuel tank. E100 fuels are “intended only for vehicles designed and certified to use it”.Officials said this is not applicable for other vehicles.“Vehicles that use E20 or normal fuel can’t use E85 or E100 fuel. Hence, the notification doesn’t require owners of existing vehicles to switch to these fuel categories or modify their vehicles now or in the future,” said a transport ministry official.TOI has learnt that the change in rules was essential for type approval and registration of FFVs on E100 considering that vehicle manufacturers are ready with their products.Depending on the vehicle’s design and certification, the range of blending may extend to E85 or E100, a fuel predominantly consisting of ethanol.Flex fuel technology is used in countries such as Brazil and the US.Ethanol has a lower fossil carbon footprint than conventional petrol and the use of higher ethanol blends can help reduce tailpipe emission of carbon monoxide (CO) and certain hydrocarbons. Greater ethanol use will also reduce dependence on import of crude oil.While govt notification will enable OEMs to manufacture FFVs, this won’t be enough to push adoption of these vehicles, experts said. This is evident as even after almost seven months of the launch of E85 cars, only 17 such vehicles have been registered.Industry players called reduction in GST on FFVs from 28% to 5% (on par with EVs) to bring down vehicle cost for buyers and compensate for mileage loss, which is about 27% while using E100 fuel.Besides, they sought a reduction in fuel cost to around Rs 75 a litre.But a bigger problem is availability of E100 given that there are only a handful of pumps, although it can run on other grades of ethanol-blended fuel.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Michigan woman Whitney Anderson, 45, buys 128-year-old abandoned church for $45,000 and turns it into dream home; spends $194,000 on renovations, hopes to finish by 2028 as total cost could reach $400,000
articles.summary: Whitney Anderson, 45, took a major financial risk when she bought a 128-year-old abandoned church in Michigan for $45,000 and began transforming it into
articles.body: Whitney Anderson, 45, took a major financial risk when she bought a 128-year-old abandoned church in Michigan for $45,000 and began transforming it into her dream home. The renovation, which started in June 2024, has already cost her an estimated $194,000, and she hopes to complete most of the work by the end of 2028.In a video feature by CNBC Make It, Anderson offers a look inside the unusual property and explains why she decided to invest her savings in a project that could cost her up to $400,000 by the time it is complete.Anderson calls her unusual home a “chouse” - a church that has been converted into a house. Despite the money and effort involved, she says the sense of peace she feels inside the building keeps her motivated.“This is still the biggest gamble I have ever made in my life,” Anderson said. She admitted that she remains uncertain whether the project will become a sustainable venture or leave her financially struggling.“It's still 50/50 if this is gonna be a sustainable chouse house, whatever you want to call it, or if it's going to be what bankrupts me. But I have this inner feeling of peace every time I'm in here. That's kind of what drives me,” she said.She left New York to find an old church to call homeAnderson lived in New York for more than 30 years before moving to Michigan in search of an old church she could convert into a home. The idea had stayed with her since childhood, when she would attend church with her grandparents.Her fascination was particularly connected to stained-glass windows and the history of buildings where communities had gathered over generations.“It wasn't necessarily a religious thing, but it was a stained glass thing,” she explained.She eventually came across a property listing on Zillow for a parsonage, a house traditionally associated with a church, which was being offered with a church included. The original asking price for the house and church was $125,000, while the lot had also been listed separately for $19,900.Anderson negotiated the price down to $45,000, citing the property's poor condition. She paid in cash, meaning she did not take out a mortgage for the purchase.She said it had taken her between three and four years to save approximately $250,000 before making the move.Renovation began with major structural problemsAnderson began work in June 2024, starting with new roofs and gutters for both the church and the accompanying house. Both buildings had significant water damage, making it essential to address leaks and moisture problems before moving on to the interiors.Although she had previous experience renovating old, abandoned and condemned properties, she described this project as a much bigger undertaking.“I just kind of looked at this as like a house flip on steroids, except I wasn't flipping this one,” she said.The challenges extended beyond the buildings themselves. After moving to a town where she did not know anyone, Anderson had to find reliable contractors and manage costs while living in a property that was still being renovated.She said she spent around a year and a half essentially camping inside the house as work continued. She also took on a substantial amount of the work herself, including demolition, installing some floor joists, laying the subfloor, doing drywall work and painting.The church's sloping floor was another major challenge. Anderson said it had an 18-inch slope and required custom 44-foot I-joists to level it. The entire building also needed to be rewired.Stained glass, old pews and a library wall give the church a new lifeWhile the renovation has involved extensive structural work, Anderson has tried to preserve the features that made her fall in love with the building in the first place.The stained-glass windows remain among her most treasured elements, although some require restoration. She said the work is expensive and will have to wait until she has saved enough money.She has also repurposed materials from the former church to create distinctive features throughout her home. Old pews were shortened to make dining chairs, while parts of the pews were used to build a library wall with bookshelves and a rolling ladder.The dining table is made largely from old pew components. In the kitchen, an old entryway door and a communion table found among the rubble were reused to create the island.Anderson has kept the main living and kitchen areas open to preserve views of the stained glass. She also exposed brick around the chimney and added conventional windows that can be opened.A pellet stove helps keep heating expenses down, while the former church space now includes living, dining, reading and creative areas. Some rooms, including parts of the rotunda and the primary bathroom, remain unfinished.‘Home Reimagined’ gave the project a helping handThe renovation received a boost when Anderson signed on to appear on Magnolia's Home Reimagined in March 2025.She said the show helped provide kitchen cabinets, appliances and countertop slabs. She paid for the fabrication and installation of the countertops, while the production also helped cover carpentry costs for the bookshelves.Anderson also credited social media with helping her reach this stage of the project, saying she would not have made as much progress without the support she received online.Despite the progress, she estimates she has spent about $194,000 on the renovation so far and is taking a break to allow her finances to recover before tackling the next major expenses.She hopes to keep the final cost below $400,000, although she acknowledged that the total remains uncertain.She hopes to open a bed and breakfast by 2028 or 2029Anderson's plans extend beyond creating a personal home. She has long wanted to run a bed and breakfast, combining her love of hosting people with her interest in travel.Her goal is to renovate the adjoining parsonage and open it to guests. She hopes to welcome her first visitors by early fall 2028, or possibly in spring 2029.The church conversion has drawn mixed reactions, particularly from people who have concerns about a former religious building being turned into a residence. Anderson said she understands those responses, but she has also encountered people who appreciate the effort to preserve the property.She said some have thanked her for saving the old building and improving the neighbourhood.For Anderson, the project remains a deeply personal decision, even as the financial risks continue.“I'm content with my decision,” she said. “I love this, I love this place, I'm head over heels in love with my chouse and nothing will change that for me.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Deadly security risks prompt updated travel warnings for 13 countries
articles.summary: Citing Iranian-backed Houthi attacks and escalation risks for Americans, the State Department has now updated advisories for 13 Middle Eastern countries.
articles.body: The U.S. State Department has updated travel advisories for several Middle Eastern countries, warning of potential armed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi forces and threats targeting Americans. Five countries — Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen — are listed under the department's highest advisory level, Level 4, which warns Americans not to travel. Eight others, including Israel, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are designated Level 3, urging travelers to reconsider their plans. AMERICANS WARNED OF KIDNAPPING, EXTORTION AS VIOLENT CRIME GRIPS PARTS OF TOURIST SPOT While the advisory levels largely remained unchanged, all 13 advisories were updated on Friday. The advisories cited recent attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis, including strikes on Riyadh's airport in Saudi Arabia and "other critical infrastructure," the department said. The attacks have resulted in civilian deaths and widespread travel disruptions, with the State Department warning that the hostilities "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area." SEXUAL ASSAULTS AND SCAMS PLAGUE TOP VACATION HOT SPOT, PROMPTING URGENT ADVISORY Americans traveling to the region also face additional risks, including health concerns in Iraq and Yemen, officials said. Kidnapping and hostage-taking were listed as additional concerns in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen, according to the State Department. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Civil unrest was also cited as a risk in Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen. The State Department encourages Americans traveling to these countries to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security alerts and updates from U.S. embassies. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Americans are also urged to monitor local news, prepare to shelter in place if conditions worsen and have an emergency departure plan that does not rely on U.S. government assistance. Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for additional information. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The updates follow several other recent travel warnings issued by the State Department. Last week, the State Department raised its travel advisory for Kenya from Level 2, "Exercise Increased Caution," to Level 3, "Reconsider Travel," citing health risks, crime, civil unrest, kidnapping and terrorism. articles.title: Chris Mason: The Budget is imminent as tricky things pile up for Burnham
articles.summary: From Brexit debates to North Sea oil, there is plenty getting the cabinet, the Labour Party and the country talking.
articles.body:
This feels like the week where the rubber hits the road for the prime minister's new government.

It is now 100 days since Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street from Buckingham Palace and began to assemble his cabinet.

Three months later, Labour MPs are more chipper, the party's poll ratings have notched up and the tone and style of government feels very different from when Sir Keir Starmer was in charge.

Coming next, though, there are a whole series of crunchy decisions and trade offs – economic and political – some of which are inevitable and some of which Burnham has decided to lean into.

You would be forgiven for only just clocking there is a Budget this week.

There are three reasons for this year's feeling like a comparatively low key affair: it is happening a month earlier than a year ago, squeezing the space available for briefings, leaks and speculation. It is considerably smaller in big picture terms – in other words the scale of tax rises – so limiting the noisy talk in advance about who might get clobbered. And the new chancellor John Healey and his team have sought to make a virtue out of not saying very much beforehand.

But woe betide suggesting to anyone involved in assembling this Budget that it is a steady-as-she-goes, nothing-to-see-here thing.

Every Budget is a big deal, goes the argument run past me by some. They don't all have to be visible from space in the way some recent ones have been – think Kwasi Kwarteng in one direction followed by Jeremy Hunt in the other four years ago, or Rachel Reeves in the last two years.

Cost of living support for some, help for entrepreneurs, more financial clout for mayors in England and an economy now recuperating will be themes for Healey on Wednesday.

You will be the judge of this Budget's scale – its value, or the lack of it to you – before long.

Next, Brexit – and our relationship with the EU

In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.

Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.

Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.

On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum.

Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that , instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.

Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate.

While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise.

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm

No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion

Some Labour MPs representing seats in the north of England and Midlands, which backed Brexit, are privately nervous about anything coming across as too enthusiastic an embrace of Brussels. A nod to that scepticism appeared to come publicly from Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood who noted that a call for an honest discussion is "not the same as settled policy".

She added: "The prime minister has also observed that there were very significant issues with freedom of movement when we were within the EU. An honest debate means actually being honest about all of the aspects of that debate and not cherry-picking."

Next month, there will be a UK-EU Summit in Brussels, which was due to happen in the summer but was postponed when Sir Keir Starmer resigned.

We can expect both sides to talk up tweaks to the current deal and the government to also, in time, set out options for what the long term relationship might look like.

On the detail, there are divisions from the cabinet and down. The key thing will be what the party decides to include or not in its next general election manifesto.

Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East.

The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

But what about the Rosebank field , 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil?

Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should.

It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it.

His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future."

Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw.

Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels?

Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government – which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see.

There is more: benefits, immigration, defence

Expected before long, the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn's review into young people and work – and with it a set of suggestions to try to cut the number of young people not in work, education or training and, in time, to try to cut the benefits bill too.

Plenty of Labour MPs acknowledge these are nettles that need grabbing, but how many may flinch when presented with the sharper edges of what might be proposed?

Meanwhile, we await where the government eventually ends up on how long migrants should have to wait to claim permanent residence in the UK .

And then, beyond what is set out in the Budget, how ministers will find the money to spend 3% of national income on defence by the end of the decade – and with what trade offs to make that happen.

There will be plenty to observe in the second 100 days of Burnham's government and beyond.

articles.title: Authorities launch manhunt for convicted killer who escaped from Tennessee prison
articles.summary: Jacob Allen Morley, 28, is alleged to have stolen a Ford F-350 flatbed truck after breaking out, state prison authorities said.
articles.body: Authorities in Tennessee launched an intense manhunt for a convicted murderer who they said escaped from a state prison, stole a work truck and remains on the loose. Jacob Allen Morley, 28, escaped from the state’s Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville sometime before he was reported missing at 11:30 p.m. Sunday, prison officials said in a statement Monday. “Further review of security cameras confirmed Morley breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform,” the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement. By 1 a.m. Monday, he is alleged to have stolen a white Ford F-350 flatbed truck in the city of about 3,500, about 100 miles north of Memphis, state law enforcement and corrections officials said. Tiptonville is near the Mississippi River and the state line with Missouri. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation placed Morley on its most-wanted list and asked residents of the city to check for any video they may have of him. “Residents are urged to check home security systems, including doorbell cameras and trail cameras, for any sightings of Morley or the stolen truck,” the bureau said in a statement. Security video shows a man in a beanie walk around the rear of the vehicle to the driver’s side door of the flatbed truck. It then shows the truck’s windshield wipers moving before the truck is driven away. Morley is 5 feet, 11 inches tall and weighs 240 pounds, the Correction Department said. It said a reward of up to $2,500 is available to anyone who has information leading to his capture. Anyone who sees him is asked to immediately call 911 or 1-800-TBI-FIND. Morley fatally shot his co-worker Cody Birchfield, 34, in the back of the head in 2022, according to court documents shared by the Carter County Clerk’s Office. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence, the documents say. Morley was convicted in February 2025 and sentenced to life behind bars. He was also convicted of abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary — the latter for stealing tools from the victim, according to the court documents. Morley was described at trial as a “loner,” the clerk’s office said. He claimed self-defense and said he had mental health issues, including bipolar disorder.

articles.title: Detransitioner says she was denied opportunity to deliver Talarico a message at CNN town hall
articles.summary: Soren Aldaco alleges she was denied an opportunity by CNN to attend a town hall and ask Texas Senate candidate James Talarico questions about his position on gender surgeries.
articles.body: Detransitioner Soren Aldaco said in an interview Monday that she tried to attend a CNN town hall with Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico earlier this month, but organizers did not respond to her request until the night before the event and allegedly told her she could not participate. During an interview on "The Katie Miller Podcast," host Katie Miller asked Aldaco, a 23-year-old detransitioner who alleged she was groomed online and subsequently pursued medical treatment as a teenager, about her criticism of Talarico and what her message to him would be. "He needs to have a long-form conversation, a real face-to-face with someone like me. And, you know, I tried to when he did the CNN town hall, where he did the 'prove me wrong' [Steven] Crowder format, engaging with constituents, right? We tried to get me in that room to talk to him about this issue and to be able to give him my message through conversation, which I think is most effective. And they actually didn't get back to us until the evening before and said, 'No, we can't get you in that room,' like 'you can't talk to him,'" Aldaco said. TALARICO DISMISSES PAST COMMENTS ABOUT GOD AND GENDER AS 'PROVOCATIVE' WHILE INVOKING CHARLIE KIRK CNN and Jubilee Media hosted a town hall with Talarico on Oct. 14, where he faced questions from the audience, as well as questions from moderator Erin Burnett. The Texas Supreme Court ruled on June 26 that Aldaco had not missed the deadline to pursue her claims against a therapist and counseling provider, reversing a lower court's finding that her lawsuit was "time-barred" under the state's two-year statute of limitations for healthcare liability claims. Miller asked her guest what she thinks Talarico is getting wrong in his positions on gender transition policies. "I think he is failing to acknowledge the repercussions of how he's been wrong in the past, because I know he's said, 'Well, I said there were six genders, and I was incorrect. I was misinformed.' And it's like, OK, but what are the repercussions of that? Because I tried to get in contact with you across five bills, four years and two sessions, and you wouldn't talk to me about bills that would have even helped people who still currently identify as trans," Aldaco told Miller. CNN did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment. Talarico was asked about his past comments referring to God as "nonbinary" and using the Bible to justify his pro-choice stance on abortion during the CNN town hall. TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS "You've said some concerning things in the past kind of related to faith and social issues. Things such as God is nonbinary, questions about how many genders there really are and your justifications using the Bible for abortion," Sarah Gardner, a Republican small business owner, said to Talarico. "And so, I think that's led a lot of Christian voters to question the authenticity of your faith. And I wanted to ask you a very direct question. Do you believe that the Bible is the absolute source of truth and God's final authoritative word, even when our culture says otherwise?" she asked. Talarico responded, "Yes." TALARICO CAMP SAYS HE OPPOSES TRANS ATHLETES IF UNSAFE OR UNFAIR BUT ACCUSES POLITICIANS OF BULLYING STUDENTS "And I think it's important to remember that even the early church, the disciples who actually knew Jesus of Nazareth, the early church, we often talk about as a singular body when, in reality, was more like early churches because there was a lot of disagreement, there was a lot of debate," he said. Talarico then went on to explain his past comments as being "provocative," drawing a parallel to his own interpretation of scripture to Charlie Kirk’s. During an interview last week, Talarico blamed Republican extremism for prompting some of his past controversial remarks, including assertions that God is "nonbinary" and that there are six biological sexes, arguing that those weren't issues he ran for office to discuss. "I was put in a position where I had to fight back against that extremism. So, you mentioned some of my comments on gender or on issues affecting trans people. It's not like I ran for the legislature to talk about these things. Again, if you go back to my first session, I wanted to talk about public education, which is why I ran in the first place," he said, pointing to other issues on which he ran. articles.title: What do you want from the Budget? 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40'
articles.summary: People earning from £380 a month to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they want to see in this year's Budget.
articles.body:
Chancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.

Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.

If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice .

Chloe's biggest worry is the cost of living. Her husband passed away four years ago and she's bringing up their 16-year-old son alone.

She's very grateful the rent for her south London maisonette is subsidised through a housing association, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."

Her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.

"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."

Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.

But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.

"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."

'I earn £22,000. Saving for a house is impossible'

Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.

Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.

"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."

Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.

He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently.

He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

Faisal Islam: Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

'I get £338 UC per month. I'm trying my best'

Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.

The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.

"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."

She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee scheme extended.

The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.

She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."

'I earn £30,000 and dread filling up my car'

Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.

He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.

He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."

The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.

"The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."

The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."

'I earn £150,000 and would be happy to pay more tax'

Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.

His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.

"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."

More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors.

"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."

'I have a £15,000 pension. I'm spending more of my savings'

Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her.

"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."

Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look at removing standing charges from gas bills , Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.

She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit , a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.

She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".

Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".

Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget

articles.title: Brazil bucks regional shift to right, brings back Lula
articles.summary: Brazilian voters have denied Latin America’s resurgent right its ultimate prize, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative presidential victories
articles.body: Brazilian voters have denied Latin America’s resurgent right its ultimate prize, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative presidential victories in 18 months. The stunning triumph of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, two days before his 81st birthday, with 51.8% of the vote to 48.2%, limits US President Donald Trump’s drive to tighten his grip on the Western Hemisphere and cements Latin America’s most populous country and largest economy as a counterweight to Washington.A Bolsonaro victory would have left Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum as the only progressive president among the region’s powerhouses.By Monday morning, with his ally Flávio Bolsonaro, following his father’s lead, refusing to concede and calling for the result to be annulled, Trump had yet to publicly acknowledge Lula’s re-election, even as congratulations poured in from around the world. PM Modi congratulated Lula on his “remarkable re-election victory” and said he is looking forward to working closely with him.For US, which has wielded tariffs, sanctions and military force to reassert its dominance in the region, Lula’s victory complicates its campaign to enlist Brazil in its military coalition against cartels.Result shows Brazil doesn’t accept to be anyone’s backyard: LulaMore broadly, Brazil’s vote opened a stretch of high-stakes elections that could reshape global politics, with Israel Tuesday holding its first national election since the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack and the US midterms on Nov 3.Yet both sides see reasons to cooperate. Washington wants access to Brazil’s vast trove of rare earths to reduce its defence industry’s reliance on China. Lula wants foreign investment and tariff relief for Brazilian exporters. “Lula is pragmatic enough to work out some kind of modus operandi with the Trump administration,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at Council on Foreign Relations, adding that the Bolsonaros’ allies in Washington would likely lose sway after the family’s second electoral defeat. Flávio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost to Lula in 2022.“I’m not sure anyone in the Trump administration, beyond a few individuals, will want to keep making the Bolsonaros the central issue in the US-Brazil relationship,” he said. Across much of Latin America, voters fed up with rising crime have rewarded presidential candidates promising to restore order. From Peru’s Keiko Fujimori to Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella and Chile’s José Antonio Kast, newly elected conservatives have courted Trump while taking their cues from El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, whose sweeping gang crackdown has sharply reduced homicides at the cost of suspended civil liberties.Trump has reinforced that shift with electoral endorsements, financial bailouts and pledges of military aid. “US is certainly putting its finger on the scale to try to help the more hardline right-wing elements in the region,” said Kenneth Roberts, a professor of govt at Cornell University.Brazil would have been Washington’s most consequential addition. Bolsonaro had promised to join the US-led security coalition “with great enthusiasm and great honour”, making his alliance with Trump part of his pitch to voters.Lula, by contrast, has championed Brazil’s long tradition of non-alignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His govt deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through Brics. Trump’s heavy-handed support for the Bolsonaros played into that message. The double-digit tariffs he imposed on a range of Brazilian goods to punish Brazil for prosecuting former President Jair Bolsonaro over a coup plot to oust Lula stirred a nationalist backlash that the leftist leader channelled into the rallying cry “Brazil belongs to Brazilians”.In his victory speech late Sunday, Lula described the outcome as “a demonstration that this country does not accept being anyone’s backyard”. Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months before the charges were annulled on procedural grounds. Lula oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment in his third term, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters felt gloomy about the high cost of living and crime.Flavio Bolsonaro (45) pitched himself as more moderate and jovial than his father and galvanised conservatives, as well as less ideological voters wanting something new. “We’re in a deep hole. People can barely afford to eat,” said 68-year-old retiree Tereza Cristina Ramos. Lula, already one of the world’s oldest leaders, will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030. He also faces a hostile Congress dominated by the right.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Romania says Russia-run sabotage network set fire near weapons factory
articles.summary: Authorities say the fire in September is part of a broader campaign against European countries that support Ukraine.
articles.body:
Romanian authorities say they have uncovered a network “coordinated” by Russia that they believe was responsible for a fire at an industrial site near a state-owned weapons factory in September.

Romania’s Intelligence Service said on Monday that the blaze in the central city of Brasov on September 14 was “part of a wider campaign of sabotage operations coordinated” by Russia amid its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The agency said the operations were aimed at arms manufacturers and “other targets of military and industrial interest”.

“These actions are intended to intimidate, undermine defence capabilities and weaken the contribution of the targeted states to European and regional security,” it said in a statement.

There was no immediate comment from Russia on Romania’s claim. Moscow has previously repeatedly denied such accusations.

Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, known as DIICOT, said three people had been involved in the Brasov fire – two Belarusians and a Ukrainian, all living in European Union countries.

Two were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offenses”, the directorate said.

According to Romania’s Intelligence Service, recruits for such networks are often found on social media and are first offered money “for a seemingly harmless task”, such as “observing or photographing certain targets”.

Over time, “the tasks become increasingly serious, potentially involving acts of vandalism, arson or even murder”, it said.

Romania, a member of the EU and NATO, shares a border of more than 600km with Ukraine.

Its centrist president, Nicusor Dan, has said the country is a target of a hybrid war that Russia is waging to destabilise nations backing Kyiv, citing drone incursions into Romanian airspace, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and sabotage.

Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said the fire in Brasov was “part of a broader campaign of sabotage across Europe” targeting military production.

“Hybrid attacks will not hold us back from strengthening our resilience and defense,” he wrote on X.

The accusation follows a string of incidents at defence sites across Europe in recent weeks.

In September, explosions and a fire erupted at an ammunition storage site in Bulgaria, weeks after a blaze at another munitions facility in the country. Both sites are operated by the Bulgarian arms maker EMCO, whose munitions are used in Ukraine.

That same month, firebombs were thrown near the offices of a defence company in Munich, and Romanian authorities said they had detained a Russian citizen accused of filming and photographing military sites in preparation for sabotage.

In August, a blast struck an ammunition factory near Rome in Italy operated by the arms maker KNDS.

At sea, at least eight cargo ships have been hit off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria over the past three weeks, and about 34 sailors have been reported dead or missing.

Dan, the Romanian president, has called the attacks on ships in Romanian waters “a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine”.

A year ago, Poland and Romania also detained eight people suspected of taking part in a Russian plot to send exploding parcels to Ukraine.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Pablo Picasso: "I put in my paintings everything I like. Too bad for the things; they only have to arrange themselves between them"
articles.summary: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who spent many years working in Paris and is popularly known as the co-founder of Cubism.
articles.body: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who spent many years working in Paris and is popularly known as the co-founder of Cubism.To date, his work is known for its unique perspective and for pushing ahead of the ordinary set rules of art, by converting unique edge shapes into something more than just brush strokes, colours, and shape.But beyond art, he also talked about profound ideas that continue to be relevant even todayEvery one of us has a pile of things we love that may be ahead of the ordinary, and then what we are told to do is be selective to pick one theme, make everything match, and we end up adjusting our lives and following the norms.Yet some of the most memorable achievements in this world have been by breaking the stereotypes people have made.Such a quote famously attributed to Pablo Pikcaso conveys this thought; he compels us to ask ourselves, do we start with what we love, or with what we think will fit?Let's know what he means to sayQuote of the dayI put in my paintings everything I like. Too bad for the things; they only have to arrange themselves between themWhat does the quote meanIn Picasso's time, a painting was expected to feel balanced and well-mannered, with objects chosen and designed accordingly because they went ‘nicely’ together. Picasso turns that rule upside down, as he began his work with love, not with harmony. If he likes something, it goes in, and the picture has to find a way to hold it.Here he jokingly says that it is "too bad for the things." He talks as if apples, cloths, and faces were guests at a dinner party who must simply learn to share a table. In the longer version of his words, he says that among things there are no class distinctions. Nothing is too plain or too odd to deserve a place on the canvas.These words belong to Picasso according to Artshorlist.com, and the longer version of the quote appears in collections of his remarks from "Conversations avec Picasso", and it mentions a painter who loves blondes but leaves them out because they don't suit a basket of fruit. But it must be noted that Picasso spoke in Spanish and French, so every English version of this quote is a translation, and words might differ from version to version,m but the meaning has hardly changed.How are these words still relevant today?Today, the digital world and our lives are more or less surrounded by ‘curated’ social media feeds that reward a proper theme; brands chase a single look; against all that, the quote feels like a new take.Think of someone who fills a room with mismatched chairs, family photos, and a loud rug, and somehow it feels warm and alive. Or a musician who mixes folk, electronic, and film music because those are the sounds they grew up with, so all that Picasso's wants to say is that originality often comes from honest taste, not from careful matching.You use AI every day. articles.title: US court rules against Trump administration in California voting case
articles.summary: US appeals court blocks government effort to stop California from tabulating ballots from list of alleged non-citizens.
articles.body:
A United States appeals court has ruled against the administration of President Donald Trump in its bid to block the state of California from counting certain mail-in ballots this election cycle.

In a decision on Monday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request from the government to sequester roughly 20,000 mailed ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm election.

The Trump administration had asserted that the ballots were sent to people who are “likely” non-citizens.

But it has not publicly revealed how it created its list or determined that the voters identified upon it were ineligible due to their citizenship status.

In a two-to-one decision, the appeals court said the Trump administration had not given lower courts enough time to review the case. It therefore declined to stop California’s ballot tabulation.

The court’s majority also underscored that election administration was the state’s responsibility under the US Constitution.

The Trump administration was asking “the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain”, Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in his opinion.

Sanchez also warned that granting the Trump administration’s petition would be “inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.

The Trump administration filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm vote on November 3.

California is a Democrat-led state, and Trump, a Republican leader, has repeatedly made unfounded claims that the state is prone to “cheating” in its elections.

The case is currently being weighed in a lower court, with a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.

But the Trump administration sought an expedited decision from the appeals court, pointing to the looming election date.

The midterm elections are critical to determine which political party holds power in Congress.

Currently, the Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, but experts project the Democratic Party is on track to make significant gains, flipping one or both chambers.

In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has raised the prospect of non-citizen voting as a threat to election integrity.

But experts say such voting is rare. California officials have likewise cast doubt on the administration’s claims of 20,000 ballots going to “likely non-citizens”, and they framed the administration’s lawsuit as an effort to interfere in the voting process.

“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing on October 20. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”

Trump’s Department of Justice has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for complete access to voter rolls that include sensitive personal data.

It has argued that releasing such information is necessary to prevent alleged voter fraud.

But the department has lost 26 of those cases thus far, with opponents successfully arguing that such manoeuvres could scare away voters and interfere with state election administration.

The Trump administration has yet to win any of the 30 cases.

Despite claims to the contrary by Trump and his allies, cases of illegal voting, including by non-citizens, are few and far between. Non-citizens are barred from participating in federal elections in all 50 states in the US.

In July, an investigation by the news service Reuters found only 129 cases of noncitizens being charged by federal authorities with illegal voting since 1996.

Many of those cases involved mistakes, like administrative errors or individuals being uncertain of voting rules, rather than fraudulent intent.

Voting rights advocates have also pointed to flaws in how the Trump administration has identified potential non-citizen voting, signalling some eligible voters may be disenfranchised as part of its efforts.

Immigration agents under Trump have been assigned to ferret out non-citizen voters, in some cases knocking on doors to inquire about the citizenship status of the residents inside.

Last week, the administration charged 28 immigrants in California with illegally voting.

But reporting from the Los Angeles Times found that some of the accused reacted to the charges with confusion and maintained that they never registered to vote.

Trump has a history of promoting false claims of election fraud in order to justify greater federal influence over the voting process.

In 2020, he lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he denied his defeat, instead blaming vote “rigging”. That claim prompted some of Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2023, in an apparent effort to halt the election certification.
